# Sharp simultaneous cap loss under contraction about the actual centroid

This is an ordinary convex-geometric theorem. It provides a quantitative
input for the actual endpoint-contraction certificate; no general
mixed-integer depth conclusion is asserted.

## Theorem and definitions

Let d>=1 and let A be a convex body in R^d. Put a=vol_d(A)>0 and
g=a^(-1) integral_A x dx. For a nonzero normal v and a proper cutting
level b, meaning min_A v.x<b<max_A v.x, put

    U=|A intersect {v.x>=b}|,
    sigma=H_(d-1)(A intersect {v.x=b})/||v||.

Thus 0<U<a and sigma>0. In dimension1 the numerator is H_0=1,
so sigma=1/||v||. Define the nested homothetic contraction

    A_epsilon=g+(1-epsilon)(A-g), 0<=epsilon<1.

Its cap-loss right derivative exists and equals

    L_g=lim_(epsilon down to0)
          [U-|A_epsilon intersect {v.x>=b}|]/epsilon
       =dU+(b-v.g)sigma.                                     (1)

The following sharp inequality holds:

    L_g >= [d^2/(d+1)] a^(1/d) U^((d-1)/d).                  (2)

For every d>=1 and every fraction 0<U/a<1, an actual full-dimensional
cone (an interval for d=1) attains equality at a proper parallel cut.
The point g is the SAME point for every choice of cap on A.

## 1. Proper sections and cap-root concavity

Use the scalar coordinate t=v.x-b and define

    F(t)=|A intersect {v.x-b>=t}|.

Let ell=min_A(v.x-b)<0 and h=max_A(v.x-b)>0. Then F(t)=a for
t<=ell, F(t)=0 for t>=h, and F(0)=U. For d>=2, the section-volume
function divided by ||v|| is continuous and positive on (ell,h).
Indeed the sections satisfy the ordinary (d-1)-dimensional
Brunn--Minkowski concavity inequality; its positive root is a finite
concave function on the open interval and hence is continuous there.
For d=2 this is simply concavity of interval length. In dimension1
the proper section density is the constant 1/||v||. Fubini's theorem
therefore gives F'(0)=-sigma in every dimension considered.

For any t_1,t_2<h and 0<=theta<=1, actual convexity supplies

    (1-theta)(A intersect {v.x-b>=t_1})
       +theta(A intersect {v.x-b>=t_2})
       subset A intersect {v.x-b>=(1-theta)t_1+theta t_2}.

The ordinary d-dimensional Brunn--Minkowski inequality shows that
F^(1/d) is concave on (-infinity,h). This includes its constant part
to the left of ell. Its tangent at0 is consequently an upper bound
throughout that interval:

    F(t)^(1/d) <= U^(1/d) - sigma t/[d U^((d-1)/d)].       (3)

Put

    D=dU/sigma>0,   s=(a/U)^(1/d)>1,
    t_0=D(1-s)<0.

If h>D, applying (3) at some t strictly between D and h would bound
a positive number by a negative one. Therefore h<=D. It follows,
including t above actual support where F is zero, that

    F(t)<=U(1-t/D)^d for 0<=t<=D.                         (4)

For t_0<=t<=0 the tangent is nonnegative, so the same upper bound
holds by (3). Together with F<=a, this gives

    a-F(t)>=a-U(1-t/D)^d>=0,  t_0<=t<=0.                 (5)

No assertion that either support endpoint equals its tangent bound
has been used.

## 2. Signed first moment, with both tails retained

The mean of the scalar coordinate is mu=v.g-b. Applying layer cake
to its positive and negative parts gives exactly

    a mu=integral_0^infinity F(t)dt
               -integral_(-infinity)^0 [a-F(t)]dt.       (6)

All integrals are finite because A is bounded. Hyperplane boundaries
are null for d-volume, including in dimension1, so the convention
of closed caps makes no difference in this identity.

Using (4) on the positive integral and (5) on a SUBINTERVAL of the
nonnegative subtracted integral,

    a mu <= integral_0^D U(1-t/D)^d dt
                -integral_(D(1-s))^0 [a-U(1-t/D)^d]dt
          = UD/(d+1) - aD(s-1)
                + UD(s^(d+1)-1)/(d+1)
          = aD[1-ds/(d+1)].                             (7)

In the last equality, U s^d=a. This step retains the uncaptured
part's first moment; omitting that part would lose the sharp power
of U.

The exact homothety formula for the cap is

    |A_epsilon intersect {v.x>=b}|
       =(1-epsilon)^d
          |A intersect {v.x>=(b-epsilon v.g)/(1-epsilon)}|.

Proper-section differentiability proves (1). Combining (1) and (7),

    L_g=dU-sigma mu
       >=dU-dU[1-ds/(d+1)]
       =[d^2/(d+1)] U s,

which is (2). First g belongs to A: otherwise strict separation of a
point from a compact convex set would contradict v.g=average_A v.x<=h_A(v).
The centroid belongs to int A: if a nonzero supporting
functional attained its maximum at g on the boundary, its strictly
smaller values throughout int A would contradict its mean. Thus the
specified contractions are actual nested bodies about an admissible
point, and no center outside A has entered the argument.

## 3. Sharpness for every proper cap fraction

For d>=2 take a (d-1)-dimensional convex body E in a hyperplane
t=t_0, and take one apex at height D>0. Its convex hull is a
full-dimensional cone with volume a after choosing the base measure.
Prescribe p=U/a in (0,1), set s=p^(-1/d), and choose t_0=D(1-s).
The coordinate t here may be an ordinary unit coordinate. The exact
upper tail on [t_0,D] is

    F(t)=a[(D-t)/(D-t_0)]^d=U(1-t/D)^d.

It is constant a below t_0 and zero above D. Hence both inequalities
used in (7) are equalities, and (2) is an equality. The cut t=0 is
proper because t_0<0<D. In dimension1 use the interval [t_0,D];
the same calculation is valid and gives L_g=a/2 for every proper cut.
Only positive U is used, so its exponent0 causes no 0^0 issue.

## 4. Simultaneous weighted and mixed-fiber consequences

For any finite family of proper caps of this same A, and any
nonnegative weights w_i, summing (2) gives at ONE actual point g

    sum_i w_i L_i(g)
       >=[d^2/(d+1)] a^(1/d) sum_i w_i U_i^((d-1)/d).     (8)

One does not maximize the different losses at different points.
In the planar three-fiber fixed-facet certificate of
`candidate 0e094dd9f76aefdd`,
put pi_i=lambda_i/sum_j lambda_j. Equations (2) and (8) show that

    Lbar(g_A)>=(4/3)a sum_i pi_i sqrt(U_i/a).              (9)

Consequently sum_i pi_i sqrt(U_i/a)>=1/3 supplies its sufficient
loss threshold Lbar>=4a/9. When its separate actual-global-maximality,
proper-cut and strict endpoint-gap hypotheses hold and Q/M<2/9,
this gives the strict normalized descent proved in that source.

The weighted square-root condition is not claimed to follow from
the cap-cover condition alone or from a small endpoint volume. Tied
endpoint sources still require the separate two-rate criterion. The
ordinary result (2) and its sharpness hold independently of any of
these additional mixed-fiber hypotheses.

## 5. Exact profile-deficit identity

Define the comparison survival function on the whole real line by

    F_cone(t)=min{a,U(1-t/D)_+^d}.

The preceding tangent proof gives F<=F_cone everywhere. Both functions
are a sufficiently far to the left and zero sufficiently far to the
right, so their nonnegative difference has compact support. Applying
the signed first-moment formula to both distributions gives the exact
identity

    L_g-[d^2/(d+1)] a^(1/d) U^((d-1)/d)
       =(sigma/a) integral_R [F_cone(t)-F(t)]dt.            (10)

This records the actual geometric slack in (2). It is not a claim
that deficits from unrelated bodies or independently chosen cuts can
be freely allocated. In a simultaneous weighted sum, each F is the
actual directional cap profile of the one body A.
